design_detail: Systematic review without meta-analysis, described as following PRISMA, of animal and human studies of cognitive impairment after clinical or recreational GHB use, in three themes: animal studies, acute effects in humans, and residual impairment after GHB use and GHB-induced comas. PubMed, PsycINFO and Google Scholar searched to August 2020; 43 reports included (24 animal, 14 human acute, and reports on lasting effects from one Dutch research programme); narrative synthesis with two summary tables.
can_establish: Which studies up to August 2020 the authors found on GHB and cognition, what those studies reported as summarized (acute memory and psychomotor impairment in laboratory studies; lasting differences in one cross-sectional sample of people with heavy use and repeated comas), and the absence of any human follow-up study of whether such differences reverse.
cannot_establish: Whether GHB or GHB-induced comas cause lasting cognitive impairment (the human evidence on lasting effects is one cross-sectional sample, which the authors say may reflect differences that predate use); the size of any effect (no pooling, no effect sizes); how thinking is the day after a single occasional dose (no human study of next-day effects is reported); and the completeness of the evidence (limited search, no appraisal of included studies).

sample.recruitment: PsycINFO, PubMed and Google Scholar searched to August 2020 with terms for GHB, cognitive impairment (including learning and memory) and GHB-induced unconsciousness, plus reference lists of included studies and reviews; 244 records, 215 after removing duplicates, 36 selected on title and abstract, 43 after reference screening (Methods › Approach; Study Selection). The search string and PRISMA checklist are in a supplement that was not read.
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Studies of the effect of, or association between, GHB use and cognitive impairment, in Dutch, English, German or French. Excluded: human studies with fewer than 8 participants, reviews, non-controlled studies, comments and case reports.
sample.demographics: Human acute studies: 8 to 49 participants each (Table 2), volunteers with or without drug-use histories. Lasting-effects sample: 81 participants in three equal groups (heavy GHB use with repeated GHB-induced comas; regular GHB use without comas; people with mild polydrug use who had never used GHB). Animal studies mostly in rats, with mice, chickens and monkeys.
sample.attrition: Not applicable at review level; not reported for the primary studies.
sample.selection_effects: Narrow search (three sources, four languages, no grey literature or registries). The 2018 placebo-controlled GHB driving-simulator study by Liakoni et al., published within the search window and including a divided-attention task, is not among the acute studies. Surveys, post-marketing reports and reports from victims of drug-facilitated assault are used in the text although non-controlled studies were an exclusion criterion.

exposure.measurement: Varies by study: laboratory administration in the acute human studies and animal studies; self-reported GHB use and self-reported GHB-induced comas in the lasting-effects sample; clinical prescription in narcolepsy reports.
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Study conditions as summarized: acute human studies gave single oral doses from about 10 to 140 mg/kg (expressed in various ways, for example 2.5 g/70 kg or 1 to 10 g/70 kg; Table 2); animal studies mostly 10 to 1000 mg/kg intraperitoneally or by mouth (Table 1). The lasting-effects groups were defined as heavy use (at least 25 times in the preceding two years) with at least four GHB-induced comas, regular moderate use without any coma, and controls who had never used GHB. Narcolepsy treatment 4.5 to 9 g a day in two doses. The review gives common recreational amounts in its introduction; they are not study conditions and are not repeated here.
exposure.polysubstance: The control group in the lasting-effects sample was chosen as people with mild polydrug use because polysubstance use is common among people who use GHB; whether the GHB groups' other drug and alcohol use was matched or adjusted for is not reported in the review.
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Not reported for the lasting-effects sample; no follow-up after stopping GHB exists, according to the authors.

comparison.controls: Acute studies: placebo or comparator drugs (triazolam, pentobarbital, alcohol) as summarized. Lasting effects: regular GHB use without comas, and people with mild polydrug use who never used GHB.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: The authors state that brain abnormalities in the heavy-use group may have been present before GHB use and may be a risk factor for it; premorbid cognition, education and psychiatric history are not reported.
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: Controls were people with mild polydrug use; differences in amount of other drug use are not reported.

outcomes.instruments: As summarized: digit symbol substitution, memory tasks (word recall, digit retention, episodic and working memory), psychomotor and vigilance tasks, critical flicker fusion; in the lasting-effects sample, neuropsychological tests, structural MRI and diffusion imaging, task-based and resting-state functional MRI, and self-reported anxiety, stress, depression and impulsivity; animal memory, learning and gene-expression measures.
outcomes.operationalization: Cognitive impairment is treated broadly, from acute amnesia during intoxication to lasting differences in memory and brain function between groups.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not reported for the primary studies.

analysis.effect_sizes: None reported. The review summarizes direction only: impaired performance in most acute human studies at moderate or higher doses, little or no effect at the lowest doses tested, memory impairment smaller than with triazolam, pentobarbital or alcohol at the doses compared; in surveys, 13% and 45% of the people who used GHB daily in one sample (42 people) reported amnesia during and after use, and all 51 people who used GHB regularly in another reported anterograde amnesia, with 29% reporting impaired memory and 41% passing out after use; in the lasting-effects sample, the heavy-use-with-comas group performed worst on verbal memory and reported more anxiety, stress, depression and impulsivity.
analysis.preregistration_detail: No protocol or registration is mentioned; the review states it was conducted using PRISMA.
analysis.selective_reporting: No appraisal or structured extraction; the selection of findings described in the text is the authors'. Conflicting animal findings (neuroprotection in ischaemia models; no working-memory effect in some studies) are reported briefly.

interpretation_gap.results_show: Laboratory studies, as summarized, show that GHB impairs memory and psychomotor performance while it acts, roughly in proportion to dose. One cross-sectional Dutch sample of 81 people found worse verbal memory, more self-reported anxiety, stress, depression and impulsivity, and brain differences in people with heavy use and repeated GHB-induced comas than in people with regular use without comas and polydrug controls. No human study has followed people over time, and none measured thinking in the days after a single dose.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract states that regular high-dose GHB use and repeated GHB-induced comas are probably neurotoxic, resulting in long-term residual cognitive impairment, and the conclusion that the results consistently show acute and long-lasting impairment. Gaps: (1) the human evidence for lasting effects is a single cross-sectional sample reported in six papers by a group that includes two of this review's authors, which the review does not flag; (2) the discussion itself notes that the differences may predate GHB use and that reversibility is unknown, but the abstract and conclusion speak of neurotoxicity; (3) ‘consistently’ is not supported where the animal evidence includes neuroprotective findings and there is only one human sample; (4) no study was appraised for bias.

timeline.event: Raposo Pereira et al. first reports from the Dutch sample of regular GHB use with and without GHB-induced comas (long-term memory; dorsolateral prefrontal function), as cited by this review.
Liakoni et al. placebo-controlled GHB driving-simulator study, not included in this review
Further reports from the same Dutch sample (brain structure and impulsivity; resting-state connectivity; demographic and clinical characteristics), as cited by this review.

replication.where_it_stands: The only review of GHB and cognition in the papers read for this card. Its account of lasting effects rests entirely on one cross-sectional sample from the authors' own network; acute laboratory impairment is well described in the primary studies it lists. Independent, longitudinal human data on lasting effects do not exist in the evidence it found.

funding.declared_conflicts: The authors declare no conflict of interest, financial or otherwise.
funding.affiliations_note: Two authors (F. R. Pereira, as Raposo Pereira, and W. van den Brink) are authors of the six reports from the Dutch sample on which the review's conclusions about lasting effects rest; the review does not discuss this.

what_would_settle_it: A prospective cohort of people who use GHB, with cognitive testing and imaging at entry and repeatedly over years, recording GHB-induced comas, other drug and alcohol use and premorbid factors, and including people who stop; and a placebo-controlled laboratory study of thinking the day after a single dose.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: Five critical items are 'no' (2 protocol, 4 search, 7 excluded studies, 9 risk of bias, 13 interpretation), which under AMSTAR 2 gives critically low confidence: the review should not be relied on as a comprehensive or unbiased summary. It may be cited as a pointer to the acute laboratory studies it lists (whose results should be taken from the primary papers), for the fact that the human evidence on lasting effects up to 2020 is one cross-sectional sample, and for the authors' statement that no human follow-up study exists; it should not be cited for neurotoxicity or for a causal effect of GHB-induced comas on memory.

key_findings.finding: 43 reports were included: 24 animal studies, 14 human studies of acute effects, and studies of lasting effects of GHB use and GHB-induced comas; the lasting-effects evidence comes from one research programme (six reports cited) on one sample of 81 participants.
key_findings.locator: Methods › 2.3 Study Selection, 1st paragraph; Results, 1st paragraph; Results › 3.3, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: In the 14 acute human laboratory studies (8 to 49 participants each), GHB impaired digit-symbol, memory and psychomotor performance at moderate and higher doses; at the lowest doses tested it had modest or no effects; at the doses compared its memory impairment was less than that of triazolam, pentobarbital or alcohol and shorter-lived than that of alcohol.
key_findings.locator: Results › 3.2 Acute Effect of GHB on Cognition in Human Studies, 2nd paragraph; Table 2

key_findings.finding: In surveys summarized by the review, 13% and 45% of the people who used GHB daily in a sample of 42 reported amnesia during and after use, and all 51 people who used GHB regularly in another sample reported anterograde amnesia, 29% having experienced impaired memory and 41% passing out after use.

In the Dutch sample of 81 (three equal groups: heavy use with repeated GHB-induced comas; regular use without comas; polydrug controls who never used GHB), the coma group performed worst on verbal memory, reported more anxiety, stress, depression and impulsivity, and showed differences in memory-encoding and working-memory brain activity; the group without comas showed resting-state connectivity differences from controls.
key_findings.locator: Results › 3.3 Residual Cognitive Impairment Following GHB-Use and GHB-Induced Comas, 1st to 3rd paragraphs

key_findings.finding: The authors state that no follow-up study after stopping GHB has been done, so it is unknown whether the differences reverse, and that the brain abnormalities may have been present before GHB use and may have been a risk factor for it.

In clinical use for narcolepsy, side effects are summarized as generally mild and reversible (nausea, headache, insomnia, dizziness); post-marketing data mention impaired attention and working memory at unknown frequency, more often with valproic acid; the authors attribute the near-absence of cognitive complaints in patients to tolerance.

Animal studies, as summarized, report memory and learning impairment, neuronal loss in prefrontal cortex and hippocampus after repeated GHB, and changes in genes for oxidative stress, but other studies report neuroprotective effects in ischaemia models and no working-memory effect in rats or monkeys.
key_findings.locator: Results › 3.1 Animal Studies, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Table 1

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract names PubMed and PsycINFO as the sources searched; the Methods add Google Scholar.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor inconsistency in the search description.

reporting_issues.issue: Non-controlled studies and case reports are exclusion criteria, yet the Results rely on uncontrolled surveys, post-marketing data and reports from victims of drug-facilitated assault.
reporting_issues.consequence: The eligibility criteria were not applied as stated; the survey figures are not from controlled studies.

reporting_issues.issue: The Results count 5 studies of lasting effects, but the text cites six reports from one sample of 81 participants.
reporting_issues.consequence: The lasting-effects evidence should be counted as one sample, not five independent studies.

reporting_issues.issue: The conclusion says the summarized results consistently show long-lasting impairment, while the review's own text reports one cross-sectional sample, no follow-up, and conflicting animal findings.
reporting_issues.consequence: The conclusion overstates the consistency and strength of the evidence.
